gz3_uprising.topic: The First Intifada and the birth of Hamas

claims.text: The First Intifada began on 9 December 1987 in Jabalia camp, after an Israeli truck crashed into cars carrying Palestinian workers on 8 December, killing four, three of them from the camp; rumors that it was deliberate were denied by Israel; on 9 December soldiers fired on stone-throwers and killed 17-year-old Hatem al-Sisi.

In the first year, 142 Palestinians were killed in Gaza and no Israelis there (77 shot, 37 from tear-gas inhalation, 17 from beatings); one calculation gives 60,706 Gazans injured 1988–1993; tear gas was used heavily in camps including al-Shati, Jabalia and Bureij.

Over the uprising B'Tselem counts 1,087 to 1,204 Palestinians killed by Israeli forces (about 241 children) and 179 Israelis killed (official Israeli figure 200); an estimated 771 (AP) to 942 (IDF) Palestinians were killed by Palestinians as alleged collaborators; arrests are estimated at 57,000–120,000; 481 deported; 1,882–2,532 homes demolished; Rabin adopted a policy of 'might, power and beatings'.

Hamas emerged from the Mujama al-Islamiya charity founded by Ahmed Yassin in 1973, affiliated with the Muslim Brotherhood; it gives its founding as 10 December 1987; its charter, signed 18 August 1988, called for an Islamic state in all of Palestine and rejected a two-state solution; its 2017 'Document of General Principles' accepted a state on the 1967 lines without recognizing Israel and did not formally repudiate the charter; Rashid Khalidi and the Times of Israel are cited for the view that Israel initially discreetly supported it as a counterweight to the PLO.

The Agreement on the Gaza Strip and the Jericho Area was signed on 4 May 1994 by Arafat and Rabin; it created the Palestinian Authority, provided for a partial Israeli withdrawal from Gaza and Jericho within three weeks while Israeli troops stayed at the Rafah crossing and the settlements, included the Paris Protocol on economic relations and established the Palestinian police; Arafat returned to Gaza City on 1 July 1994, his first visit in 25 years, and the PA was inaugurated in Jericho on 5 July; the agreement was superseded by Oslo II in 1995.
In the early 1990s Israel imposed a closure regime under which Palestinian workers needed permits subject to security clearance; the Oslo Accords did not end it.

The Declaration of Principles was signed in Washington on 13 September 1993; it provided for Palestinian self-government for a transitional period of up to five years, beginning with Israeli withdrawal from Gaza and Jericho, with permanent-status talks (Jerusalem, refugees, settlements, security, borders) to begin by the third year; the interim period was to end on 4 May 1999.

The Second Intifada began on 28 September 2000 after Ariel Sharon's visit to the Temple Mount/Haram al-Sharif and is usually dated to the Sharm el-Sheikh truce of 8 February 2005; B'Tselem counted (to April 2008) 4,745 Palestinians killed by Israeli security forces, 44 by Israeli civilians, 577 by Palestinians, and about 1,053 Israelis killed by Palestinians; Qassam rockets and mortars were fired from Gaza at Israeli communities including Sderot; HRW reported over 1,500 houses destroyed in Rafah operations; 90 smuggling tunnels were found September 2000–May 2004.

claims.text: Sharon presented the disengagement plan on 18 December 2003 and set it out in a letter to President Bush on 14 April 2004; Likud members rejected it in a referendum on 2 May 2004 (65% against); the cabinet approved an amended plan 14–7 on 6 June 2004; the Knesset gave preliminary approval 67–45 on 26 October 2004 and passed the Implementation Law 59–40 on 16 February 2005.

The 21 Gaza settlements were evacuated 15–22 August 2005, with about 8,000 settlers removed and two-thirds accepting compensation; demolition crews razed about 2,800 homes and buildings; the last soldier left on 12 September 2005; Egypt was allowed 750 border guards on the Philadelphi corridor; total cost about $2 billion.

After 2005 Israel retained control of Gaza's airspace and territorial waters, six of its seven land crossings, the population registry and the right to re-enter militarily, and Gaza remained dependent on Israel for water, electricity and telecommunications; the UN, human rights groups and most legal scholars hold that Gaza remained occupied (affirmed in the ICJ's 2024 opinion); Israel says the occupation ended and called Gaza a 'hostile entity'; scholars disagree (Shany: probably not occupied; Dinstein: still occupied).

In a Haaretz interview on 6 October 2004, Sharon's adviser Dov Weisglass said the disengagement 'supplies the amount of formaldehyde' needed so that there would be no political process with the Palestinians, and described it as freezing the peace process.
